8	# Security and Reliability Checklist
9	
10	## Contents
11	- Input/Output Safety (XSS, injection, SSRF, path traversal, unsafe deserialization)
12	- AuthN/AuthZ
13	- JWT & Token Security
14	- Secrets and PII
15	- Supply Chain & Dependencies
16	- CORS & Headers
17	- Runtime Risks (unbounded ops, GIL contention, resource exhaustion)
18	- Cryptography
19	- Race Conditions (shared state, TOCTOU, database concurrency, distributed)
20	- Data Integrity
21	
22	## Input/Output Safety
23	
24	- **XSS**: Unsafe HTML injection, Jinja2 `|safe` filter or `Markup()` bypassing auto-escaping, raw string interpolation in HTML responses
25	- **Injection**: SQL injection via f-strings or `%` formatting instead of parameterized queries; command injection via `os.system`, `subprocess.run(shell=True)` with user input
26	- **SSRF**: User-controlled URLs reaching internal services without allowlist validation
27	- **Path traversal**: User input in file paths without sanitization (`../` attacks), `os.path.join` with absolute user input bypassing base directory
28	- **Unsafe deserialization**: Using `pickle.loads`, `yaml.load` (without `SafeLoader`), or `eval`/`exec` on untrusted input
29	- **Code injection via imports**: User input reaching `__import__`, `importlib.import_module`, or dynamic module loading
30	
31	## AuthN/AuthZ
32	
33	- Missing tenant or ownership checks for read/write operations
34	- New endpoints without auth guards or RBAC enforcement
35	- Trusting client-provided roles/flags/IDs
36	- Broken access control (IDOR - Insecure Direct Object Reference)
37	- Session fixation or weak session management
38	
39	## JWT & Token Security
40	
41	- Algorithm confusion attacks (accepting `none` or `HS256` when expecting `RS256`)
42	- Weak or hardcoded secrets
43	- Missing expiration (`exp`) or not validating it
44	- Sensitive data in JWT payload (tokens are base64, not encrypted)
45	- Not validating `iss` (issuer) or `aud` (audience)
46	
47	## Secrets and PII
48	
49	- API keys, tokens, or credentials in code/config/logs
50	- Secrets in git history or environment variables exposed to client
51	- Excessive logging of PII or sensitive payloads
52	- Missing data masking in error messages
53	
54	## Supply Chain & Dependencies
55	
56	- Unpinned dependencies allowing malicious updates (missing version pins in `requirements.txt`/`pyproject.toml`)
57	- Dependency confusion (private package name collision on PyPI)
58	- Importing from untrusted sources without integrity checks
59	- Outdated dependencies with known CVEs
60	
61	## CORS & Headers
62	
63	- Overly permissive CORS (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials)
64	- Missing security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options)
65	- Exposed internal headers or stack traces
66	
67	## Runtime Risks
68	
69	- Unbounded loops, recursive calls, or large in-memory buffers
70	- Missing timeouts, retries, or rate limiting on external calls
71	- Blocking operations on the event loop (sync I/O in `async` context)
72	- Resource exhaustion (file handles, connections, memory)
73	- **`assert` stripped in optimized mode**: `python -O` removes all `assert` statements — never use `assert` for security/input validation
74	- ReDoS (Regular Expression Denial of Service)
75	
76	## Cryptography
77	
78	- Weak algorithms (MD5, SHA1 for security purposes)
79	- Hardcoded IVs or salts
80	- Using encryption without authentication (ECB mode, no HMAC)
81	- Insufficient key length
82	- Using `==` for secret/token comparison instead of `hmac.compare_digest` (leaks timing information)
83	
84	## Race Conditions
85	
86	Race conditions are subtle bugs that cause intermittent failures and security vulnerabilities. Pay special attention to:
87	
88	### Shared State Access
89	- Multiple threads accessing shared variables without locks (GIL does not protect multi-step operations)
90	- Global state or module-level mutables modified concurrently
91	- Lazy initialization without proper locking
92	- Non-thread-safe collections used in concurrent context
93	
94	### Check-Then-Act (TOCTOU)
95	- `if (exists) then use` patterns without atomic operations
96	- `if (authorized) then perform` where authorization can change
97	- File existence check followed by file operation
98	- Balance check followed by deduction (financial operations)
99	- Inventory check followed by order placement
100	- `tempfile.mktemp()` is deprecated (TOCTOU race) — use `tempfile.mkstemp()` or `NamedTemporaryFile`
101	
102	### Database Concurrency
103	- Missing optimistic locking (`version` column, `updated_at` checks)
104	- Missing pessimistic locking (`SELECT FOR UPDATE`)
105	- Read-modify-write without transaction isolation
106	- Counter increments without atomic operations (`UPDATE SET count = count + 1`)
107	- Unique constraint violations in concurrent inserts
108	
109	### Distributed Systems
110	- Missing distributed locks for shared resources
111	- Leader election race conditions
112	- Cache invalidation races (stale reads after writes)
113	- Event ordering dependencies without proper sequencing
114	- Split-brain scenarios in cluster operations
115	
116	### Common Patterns to Flag
117	```python
118	# Dangerous patterns:
119	
120	# TOCTOU
121	if not os.path.exists(path):
122	    open(path, "w").write(data)
123	
124	# Read-modify-write
125	value = cache.get(key)
126	value += 1
127	cache.set(key, value)
128	
129	# Check-then-act
130	if user.balance >= amount:
131	    user.balance -= amount
132	    user.save()
133	```
134	
135	### Questions to Ask
136	- "What happens if two requests hit this code simultaneously?"
137	- "Is this operation atomic or can it be interrupted?"
138	- "What shared state does this code access?"
139	- "How does this behave under high concurrency?"
140	
141	## Data Integrity
142	
143	- Missing transactions, partial writes, or inconsistent state updates
144	- Weak validation before persistence (implicit type conversion issues)
145	- Missing idempotency for retryable operations
146	- Lost updates due to concurrent modifications
147	
148	END SOURCE

154	# SOLID Smell Prompts
155	
156	## SRP (Single Responsibility)
157	
158	- File owns unrelated concerns (e.g., HTTP + DB + domain rules in one file)
159	- Large class/module with low cohesion or multiple reasons to change
160	- Functions that orchestrate many unrelated steps
161	- God objects that know too much about the system
162	- Circular imports between modules (signals tangled responsibilities — causes `ImportError`/`AttributeError` at runtime)
163	- **Ask**: "What is the single reason this module would change?"
164	
165	## OCP (Open/Closed)
166	
167	- Adding a new behavior requires editing many `if/elif` chains (or `match/case` blocks)
168	- Feature growth requires modifying core logic rather than extending
169	- No plugin/strategy/hook points for variation
170	- **Ask**: "Can I add a new variant without touching existing code?"
171	
172	## LSP (Liskov Substitution)
173	
174	- Subclass checks for concrete type via `isinstance` or raises for base method
175	- Overridden methods weaken preconditions or strengthen postconditions
176	- Subclass ignores or no-ops parent behavior
177	- **Ask**: "Can I substitute any subclass without the caller knowing?"
178	
179	## ISP (Interface Segregation)
180	
181	- ABCs/Protocols with many methods, most unused by implementers
182	- Callers depend on broad interfaces for narrow needs
183	- `NotImplementedError` stubs in subclasses
184	- **Ask**: "Do all implementers use all methods?"
185	
186	## DIP (Dependency Inversion)
187	
188	- High-level logic depends on concrete IO, storage, or network types
189	- Hard-coded implementations instead of abstractions or injection
190	- Import chains that couple business logic to infrastructure
191	- **Ask**: "Can I swap the implementation without changing business logic?"
192	
193	---
194	
195	## Common Code Smells (Beyond SOLID)
196	
197	| Smell | Signs |
198	|-------|-------|
199	| **Long method** | Function > 30 lines, multiple levels of nesting |
200	| **Feature envy** | Method uses more data from another class than its own |
201	| **Data clumps** | Same group of parameters passed together repeatedly |
202	| **Primitive obsession** | Using strings/numbers instead of domain types |
203	| **Shotgun surgery** | One change requires edits across many files |
204	| **Divergent change** | One file changes for many unrelated reasons |
205	| **Dead code** | Unreachable or never-called code |
206	| **Speculative generality** | Abstractions for hypothetical future needs |
207	| **Magic numbers/strings** | Hardcoded values without named constants |
208	| **Expensive `@property`** | Property getter performs I/O, DB queries, or heavy computation — callers expect attribute access to be cheap |
209	
210	---
211	
212	## Refactor Heuristics
213	
214	1. **Split by responsibility, not by size** - A small file can still violate SRP
215	2. **Introduce abstraction only when needed** - Wait for the second use case
216	3. **Keep refactors incremental** - Isolate behavior before moving
217	4. **Preserve behavior first** - Add tests before restructuring
218	5. **Name things by intent** - If naming is hard, the abstraction might be wrong
219	6. **Prefer composition over inheritance** - Multiple inheritance creates MRO complexity and tight coupling
220	7. **Make illegal states unrepresentable** - Use types to enforce invariants
221	
222	END SOURCE

228	# Code Quality Checklist
229	
230	## Contents
231	- Error Handling (anti-patterns, best practices, questions)
232	- Performance & Caching (CPU, database/IO, caching, memory)
233	- Boundary Conditions (None handling, empty collections, numeric, string)
234	
235	## Error Handling
236	
237	### Anti-patterns to Flag
238	
239	- **Swallowed exceptions**: Empty `except` blocks or catch with only logging. Example:
240	  ```python
241	  try: ...
242	  except Exception: pass              # Silent failure
243	  try: ...
244	  except Exception as e: print(e)     # Log and forget, no re-raise
245	  ```
246	- **Overly broad except**: Catching bare `Exception` or `BaseException` instead of specific types
247	- **Error information leakage**: Stack traces or internal details exposed to users
248	- **Missing error handling**: No try-except around fallible operations (I/O, network, parsing)
249	- **Async error handling**: Unhandled exceptions in `asyncio` tasks, missing `try/except` in coroutines, fire-and-forget tasks without error callbacks
250	
251	### Best Practices to Check
252	
253	- [ ] Errors are caught at appropriate boundaries
254	- [ ] Error messages are user-friendly (no internal details exposed)
255	- [ ] Errors are logged with sufficient context for debugging
256	- [ ] Async task exceptions are retrieved or handled (not silently dropped)
257	- [ ] Fallback behavior is defined for recoverable errors
258	- [ ] Critical errors trigger alerts/monitoring
259	
260	### Questions to Ask
261	- "What happens when this operation fails?"
262	- "Will the caller know something went wrong?"
263	- "Is there enough context to debug this error?"
264	
265	---
266	
267	## Performance & Caching
268	
269	### CPU-Intensive Operations
270	
271	- **Expensive operations in hot paths**: `re.compile` in loops, JSON parsing in hot paths, crypto in loops
272	- **Blocking the event loop**: Sync I/O or heavy computation in `async` functions without `run_in_executor`
273	- **Unnecessary recomputation**: Same calculation done multiple times
274	- **Missing caching**: Pure functions called repeatedly with same inputs, no `@functools.lru_cache` or `@functools.cache`
275	- **GIL limitation for CPU-bound work**: `threading` does not parallelize CPU-bound tasks due to the GIL — use `multiprocessing` or `concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor`
276	
277	### Database & I/O
278	
279	- **N+1 queries**: Loop that makes a query per item instead of batch
280	  ```python
281	  # Bad: N+1
282	  for id in ids:
283	      user = db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", (id,)).fetchone()
284	
285	  # Good: Batch
286	  users = db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN %s", (tuple(ids),)).fetchall()
287	  ```
288
